title: Femoral wall thickness follows the bending-moment distribution along the shaft

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Femoral wall thickness follows the bending-moment distribution along the shaft

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because bending strain is greatest at mid-length of a bent column, the walls of a long bone such as the femur are thickest in the middle of the shaft and thin gradually towards the ends, so that wall thickness forms a graph of the bending moments along the bone.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: wall thickness t(x) \propto bending moment M(x), maximal at mid-shaft

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Hence, if our cylindrical column be exposed to strong bending stresses, it will be prudent and economical to make its walls thickest in the middle and thinning off gradually towards the ends; and if we look at a longitudinal section of a thigh-bone, we shall see that this is just what nature has done.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVI, “On Form and Mechanical Efficiency”; topic “Tubular construction of bones and stems”. Scope: weight-bearing long bones, especially the human femur

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: wall thickness t(x) \propto bending moment M(x), maximal at mid-shaft

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch16-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.78

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The predicted profile is quantitative and scan analysis is straightforward. Available imaging can test humans and selected taxa, but estimating subject-specific bending moments and covering weight-bearing bones broadly limits resolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Extract cortical wall thickness along CT-scanned femora and compare its longitudinal profile with bending moments from musculoskeletal or beam models. Correlation after accounting for axial and torsional loads supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Muscle forces and habitual loading are usually not paired with bone scans.

Epiphyses and shaft are subject to multiple load modes.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Open whole-femur CT is sufficient to test the descriptive claim that human femoral walls are thickest at midshaft and thin toward the ends. Matching that profile to a bending-moment graph requires a load model, and more than one plausible model moves the peak. The human femur, which is Thompson's central case, is therefore testable now, while the moment interpretation stays partly model-dependent.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Plot cortical thickness along the femoral shaft and compare it with the bending-moment diagram of a column loaded as the femur is loaded in stance. Support would be a midshaft maximum that tracks the moment and thins toward both ends; a proximal or distal maximum, or uniform walls, would refute the stated graph.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The moment diagram depends on whether the femur is treated as a simply loaded column, a cantilever, or a muscle-braced beam.

Muscle attachments and the calcar thicken the cortex locally, apart from the midshaft moment peak.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.72
discriminating power: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.58
analysis feasibility: 0.64
operationalizability: 0.8
